claims.text: Plasma nitriding of titanium alloys creates a hardened surface layer.
Plasma nitriding significantly increases the surface hardness of titanium alloys.
Plasma nitriding significantly increases the wear resistance of titanium alloys.
Typical untreated titanium alloys have moderate inherent surface hardness and wear resistance.
The proposed intervention is controlled plasma nitriding of the titanium-alloy surface.
The expected performance improvement should occur in ambient-temperature sliding wear tests under moderate loads.
The expected improvement should remain applicable at temperatures up to approximately 500°C.
Plasma nitriding forms a dense TiN layer on the titanium-alloy surface.
During plasma nitriding, nitrogen atoms diffuse into the titanium matrix.
Diffused nitrogen reacts in the titanium matrix to form TiN compounds.
The resulting TiN-containing layer is hard and wear resistant.
The nitrided layer reduces material loss under sliding contact.
Plasma nitriding is expected to increase surface hardness by approximately two- to three-fold relative to the untreated alloy.
Plasma nitriding is expected to significantly reduce wear rate relative to the untreated alloy.
Untreated titanium alloys typically have a baseline hardness of approximately 250–400 HV.
The improvement should hold under dry or minimally lubricated sliding conditions.
The improvement may not persist under severe corrosion, extreme temperatures, or highly oxidizing environments.
The degree of improvement depends on treatment time, treatment temperature, nitrogen concentration, and alloy composition.
XRD can be used to test whether TiN formed on the nitrided samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if nitrided samples fail to show at least a two-fold hardness increase and a reduction in wear rate relative to untreated controls under the specified test conditions.
